title: When (And Why) You Should Ignore Crying Students udents/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Michael Linsin addresses the instinct to comfort a crying student immediately after enforcing a consequence, arguing this well-meaning response is usually a mistake. He identifies three reasons: crying can be a manipulative tactic some students use to escape consequences, it can also represent a legitimate, valuable form of reflection that shouldn't be interrupted, and rushing to comfort a crying student teaches the rest of the class to use tears the same way. Linsin's recommendation is to leave a crying student be in the moment—regardless of whether the tears are manipulative or genuine—so the classroom management plan can do its work uninterrupted, while checking in warmly later in the day once the student has settled, through small gestures like eye contact, a smile, or an encouraging word.
points: The instinct to immediately comfort a crying student after a consequence is identified as usually counterproductive, despite being well-meaning.
Reason one: some students have learned that crying can persuade a teacher to reduce or cancel a consequence.
Reason two: crying can also be genuine, valuable self-reflection, which comforting can interrupt and undermine.
Reason three: rushing to comfort crying students teaches the rest of the class to use tears the same way to escape accountability.
The recommended approach is to leave the student be in the moment, letting the classroom management plan do its work, then check in warmly later in the day once they've settled.
quotes: But doing so in the moments after enforcing a consequence is a mistake.
Some students have learned from experience that if they cry, they have a good chance of avoiding consequence.

In any case, reflecting on their misbehavior, as well as on those who may have been affected by it, is a good thing. And the worst thing we can do is interrupt this process, sugarcoat their actions, or let them off the hook.
If every time a student cries you immediately rush to their side, then you’re going to find yourself doing it a lot.
If you make it a point to ignore crying, dramatics, and the like in the aftermath of misbehavior, then your students will stop doing it.
It’s a good idea to let them know that there are no hard feelings, that you never hold a grudge, and that forgiveness is always and forever extended.
